name: Pleurisy
preview_text: ใน TCM คุณภาพของอาการเจ็บหน้าอกของคุณ ไม่ว่าจะรุนแรงและเคลื่อนตัว แสบร้อน ถูกแทง หรือหมองคล้ำ เผยให้เห็นรูปแบบที่กระตุ้นให้เกิดเยื่อหุ้มปอดอักเสบ และแนะนำการรักษาถึงต้นตอ ...
categories: ["สภาพปอดและการหายใจ", "อาการไม่สบายหน้าอก"]
synonyms: ["Pleural Inflammation", "Pleuritic Pain", "Inflammation Of The Pleura", "Pleuritis", "Exudative pleurisy", "Exudative pleuritis"]
conventional_description: In Western medicine, pleurisy is inflammation of the pleura-the two thin layers of tissue that separate the lungs from the chest wall. Normally these layers glide smoothly against each other, but when inflamed they rub together, causing sharp chest pain that intensifies with breathing, coughing, or sneezing. The most common causes are viral infections, pneumonia, pulmonary embolism, autoimmune diseases like lupus, or chest trauma. Diagnosis typically involves listening for a pleural friction rub, chest X-rays, CT scans, and sometimes ultrasound to detect fluid buildup.
conventional_treatments: Treatment depends on the underlying cause. Bacterial infections are treated with antibiotics; viral pleurisy is managed with rest and anti-inflammatory pain relievers like ibuprofen. If a large amount of fluid accumulates (pleural effusion), doctors may drain it with a needle or chest tube. Corticosteroids may be used for autoimmune-related pleurisy. The focus is on reducing inflammation and managing pain while the body heals.
tcm_understanding:
TCM understands pleurisy primarily as a disorder of the Lung and Liver systems, with the Spleen often playing a supporting role. The Lungs govern the Qi of the chest and the smooth movement of fluids; when they are obstructed by external pathogens or internal phlegm, pain and breathlessness result. The Liver channel runs through the sides of the chest, so any disruption to the smooth flow of Liver Qi—whether from emotional stress or pathogen invasion—can manifest as rib-side pain.
The Spleen's job is to transform fluids; when it's weak, water accumulates and can settle in the pleural space as 'suspended fluid' (悬饮, xuán yǐn).
The early stage of pleurisy often begins with an external Wind invasion that gets stuck in the Shaoyang layer—a kind of 'halfway house' between the body's surface and its deep interior. This Half Exterior Half Interior pattern produces the classic alternating chills and fever, along with a dry cough and chest pain that worsens with breathing. If the pathogen is not cleared, it can generate heat and combine with internal dampness to create Phlegm-Heat in the Lungs, marked by burning pain and thick yellow sputum.
When the Spleen is already weak, fluids simply accumulate without much heat, leading to the heavy, distending pain of Phlegm-Fluids in the chest and hypochondrium.
When pleurisy lingers or recurs, the constant inflammation causes Qi and Blood to stagnate in the chest collaterals. This is the Qi and Blood Stagnation pattern—the pain becomes fixed, stabbing, and worse at night.
Over time, the heat from inflammation or the strain of fluid accumulation can deplete the body's Yin (moisture and cooling), leading to Empty-Heat with dry cough, night sweats, and afternoon fever. In elderly or debilitated patients, the opposite occurs: Yang Deficiency leaves the body cold and unable to move fluids, causing a dull ache with cold hands and fatigue.
Because each pattern has a distinct mechanism, treatment must be tailored. A formula that clears heat and phlegm will do little for a patient whose pain stems from Yang Deficiency. This is why TCM practitioners spend time distinguishing not just the location of pain, but its quality, the accompanying symptoms, and the tongue and pulse signs. The goal is to match the treatment to the person, not just the disease label.
classical_quote: 「饮后水流在胁下，咳唾引痛，谓之悬饮。」
classical_translation: "When fluid flows and lodges under the rib-side after drinking, causing pain upon coughing and spitting, it is called suspended fluid (xuan yin)."
classical_source:
Jin Gui Yao Lue (Synopsis of the Golden Chamber)  ,  Chapter 12: On Pulse, Symptom Complex, and Treatment of Phlegm-Fluid Retention Disease 									·

tcm_diagnosis:
A TCM practitioner first listens to the quality of your chest pain and asks about associated symptoms. Sharp, shifting pain that comes and goes with chills and fever points toward an early-stage external invasion, whereas a fixed, stabbing pain suggests deeper stagnation. The tongue and pulse are then checked to confirm which pattern is dominant.
In the Half Exterior Half Interior pattern, pain often alternates with chills and fever, and the chest feels tight like a band. The cough is dry or produces little phlegm, and the tongue may be slightly red with a thin coating. This pattern arises when a pathogen is trapped between the surface and interior, often in the very early stage of pleurisy.
When phlegm dominates, two distinct pictures emerge. Phlegm-Heat in the Lungs brings a burning chest pain with thick yellow sputum, dry mouth, and a rapid pulse. Phlegm-Fluids in the chest and hypochondrium produces a heavy, distending pain that worsens with coughing and deep breathing, along with breathlessness; the tongue coating is greasy and the pulse slippery. These reflect acute fluid or inflammatory congestion.
If the pain is stabbing, fixed in one spot, and worse at night, this points to Qi and Blood Stagnation. The tongue often looks dark or has purple spots, and the pulse feels choppy.
In prolonged cases, deficiency signs appear. Empty-Heat from Yin Deficiency causes a dull, lingering ache with afternoon low-grade fever and a red, peeled tongue, while Yang Deficiency leads to a cold, distending pain with a pale, swollen tongue and deep, weak pulse.

patterns.symptoms: ["Alternating chills and fever", "Chest and rib pain that worsens with coughing or deep breathing", "Bitter taste in the mouth", "Dry throat and nausea", "Irritability or feeling withdrawn"]
patterns.worse_with: Exposure to cold or wind, Emotional stress or frustration, Greasy, fried, or spicy foods, Overexertion or heavy breathing
patterns.better_with: Rest and staying warm, Warm, light meals like congee, Avoiding drafts and cold wind
patterns.why_this_happens: In the early stages of pleurisy, an external pathogen-often Wind-Cold or Wind-Heat-invades the body but fails to fully penetrate or be expelled. It lodges in the Shaoyang channel, which runs through the sides of the chest and ribcage. The struggle between the body's defensive Qi and the pathogen creates alternating chills and fever, while the constrained Qi flow in the channel produces sharp, distending pain along the ribs that worsens with coughing or deep breathing. The heat trapped in the Shaoyang dries the throat and leaves a bitter taste in the mouth.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: normal or slightly red body with redder sides, thin white or white-yellow coating. Pulse: wiry (弦 xián), taut like a guitar string.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: This pattern sits between the exterior and interior, so cold and wind can drive the pathogen deeper and worsen chills and pain. Rest and warmth help the body's Qi consolidate and push the pathogen out. Emotional stress stagnates Liver Qi, which directly affects the Shaoyang channel and intensifies rib pain, while greasy or spicy foods create internal heat and phlegm that further obstruct the chest.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat light, warm, and easily digestible foods like congee and steamed vegetables. Avoid raw, cold, greasy, or spicy foods that can trap the pathogen or generate phlegm. Keep your chest and neck protected from wind and cold, and rest until the alternating chills and fever subside.

patterns.pattern_name: Phlegm-Fluids in the chest and hypochondrium
patterns.symptoms: ["Distending, pulling pain that worsens with coughing and breathing", "Fullness and distension along the ribs on one side", "Inability to lie flat; can only lie on the affected side", "Visible bulging or swelling of the affected side of the chest", "Coughing with thin white or watery sputum"]
patterns.worse_with: Cold, raw, or greasy foods, Dairy products, Lying flat, Coughing or deep breathing, Damp or cold weather
patterns.better_with: Resting in a semi-reclined position, Lying on the affected side, Warmth on the chest, Warm, light meals like congee, Gentle breathing exercises
patterns.why_this_happens: When the body's fluid metabolism is impaired-often due to weakened Spleen and Lung function-water accumulates and congeals into pathological fluids. These fluids collect in the chest and hypochondrium, creating a condition known as 'suspended fluid' (悬饮, xuán yǐn). The fluid distends the pleural space, generating a heavy, pulling pain that sharpens with every breath or cough, and compresses the lungs so that breathing becomes shallow and rapid.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: Pale and swollen body with a white, slippery or greasy coating that is excessively moist. Pulse: Deep (Chen) and wiry (Xian), possibly slippery.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Fluid accumulation is a yin-cold pathogen that obstructs the chest and weighs down the diaphragm. Warmth and rest encourage Yang Qi to transform and move fluids, while cold and damp foods add to the internal water load. Lying on the affected side reduces tension on the pleura, easing pain, whereas lying flat or breathing deeply stretches the distended tissues and worsens the pulling sensation.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid cold, raw, and damp-producing foods such as dairy, greasy dishes, and sweets. Eat warm, cooked meals like rice congee with ginger to support Spleen Yang and fluid transformation. Rest in a semi-reclined position rather than lying flat, and keep the chest warm. Gentle breathing exercises can help, but avoid strenuous activity until the fluid resolves.

patterns.symptoms: ["Burning or scorching chest pain", "Thick, sticky yellow or green sputum", "Dry mouth with desire to drink", "Sense of heat and possible fever", "Chest tightness and breathlessness"]
patterns.worse_with: Greasy, fried, or spicy foods, Alcohol, Hot, stuffy rooms, Lying flat, Heavy dairy or sweets
patterns.better_with: Cool, fresh air, Light, non-greasy meals, Warm herbal teas, Sitting upright
patterns.why_this_happens: When phlegm and heat accumulate in the Lungs, they obstruct the normal flow of Qi and fluids in the chest. The heat inflames the pleura, causing a burning sensation, while the sticky phlegm triggers a cough that makes the pain worse. This combination of thick, yellow sputum, chest oppression, and fever reflects an acute inflammatory congestion that directly irritates the pleural lining.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body, possibly swollen at the front, with a yellow greasy coating and sometimes red prickles on the front third. Pulse: slippery (滑 huá) and rapid (数 shuò).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Spicy, greasy, and dairy-rich foods create more phlegm and heat inside the body, feeding the very congestion that inflames the pleura. Hot, stuffy air traps that heat, while lying flat limits the Lungs' ability to expand and clear phlegm. Cool, fresh air and light meals reduce the internal heat load, and sitting upright helps the Lungs descend Qi, making breathing easier and pain less intense.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid dairy, greasy, and spicy-hot foods that create more phlegm and heat. Sip warm water or pear juice, and eat light, cooling foods like radish, bamboo shoots, and water chestnuts. Gentle deep breathing and keeping the air fresh help the Lungs clear.

patterns.symptoms: ["Fixed, stabbing chest pain", "Worse at night", "Dark purple tongue with stasis spots", "Wiry and choppy pulse", "Chest tightness or oppression"]
patterns.worse_with: Stress and anger, Exposure to cold or wind, Static posture, Cold, raw, or greasy foods, Overexertion
patterns.better_with: Gentle movement, Warmth on the chest, Deep, slow breathing, Emotional calm, Rest
patterns.why_this_happens: In pleurisy, repeated inflammation or a prolonged course can cause the Qi in the chest to become stuck. When Qi stagnates for too long, the blood in the collaterals of the chest and ribs also fails to move smoothly and becomes stagnant. This blood stasis creates a fixed, stabbing pain that feels like a knife, and because blood flow naturally slows at night, the pain often worsens then.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: dark purple body with stasis spots, distended sublingual veins. Pulse: wiry (弦 xián) and choppy (涩 sè).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Blood stasis worsens when Qi flow is blocked-emotional stress knots the Qi, and cold congeals the blood. Gentle movement and warmth encourage Qi to move, which then moves blood and eases the fixed, stabbing pain.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, cooked foods that gently invigorate blood, such as turmeric, black fungus, and small amounts of onion and garlic. Avoid cold, raw, and greasy foods that can congeal blood and worsen stasis. Gentle daily movement like walking or Tai Chi keeps Qi and blood flowing. Manage stress with deep breathing, as emotional tension tightens the chest and worsens stagnation.

patterns.symptoms: ["Dull, lingering chest pain", "Low-grade fever or heat sensation in the afternoon", "Dry cough with little or no sputum", "Night sweats", "Dry mouth and throat, wanting to sip water"]
patterns.worse_with: Greasy, fried, or spicy foods, Overwork and late nights, Hot, dry weather, Emotional stress or frustration
patterns.better_with: Cool drinks and moistening foods, Rest in a cool room, Deep, slow breathing, Early nights and regular sleep
patterns.why_this_happens: In pleurisy, prolonged inflammation and fluid-heat gradually consume the body's Yin, especially the Lung and Kidney Yin that normally moisten and cool the chest. Without enough Yin, a dry, restless heat rises, leaving the pleural tissues undernourished and irritable. This produces a dull, lingering ache rather than sharp inflammation, along with classic signs of fluid depletion like dry cough and night sweats.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red, thin, and dry with cracks and little or no coating. Pulse: fine (thin) and rapid.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Yin is the body's cooling and moistening substance. When it is depleted, any heat or drying influence easily stirs up empty heat, making the chest ache and fever worse. Rest, cool drinks, and moistening foods gently rebuild Yin and settle the heat, while spicy foods and overwork consume the little Yin that remains, aggravating the pain and dryness.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Focus on moistening, Yin-nourishing foods like pear, lily bulb, honey, and congee. Avoid spicy, fried, or drying foods that stir up heat. Rest in a cool, quiet environment and avoid overwork or late nights, which deplete Yin further. Gentle breathing exercises can help keep the chest open without strain.

patterns.worse_with: Exposure to cold or wind, Overexertion, Cold, raw, or greasy foods, Damp living environment
patterns.better_with: Warmth on the chest, Rest, Warm drinks and soups, Moxibustion
patterns.why_this_happens: When the body's warming Yang Qi is too weak, it cannot transform and move fluids properly. Cold-dampness accumulates in the chest, obstructing the flow of Qi and causing a dull, heavy distending pain. This type of pleurisy often lingers in elderly or debilitated people whose internal fire is already low.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, swollen, moist with teeth marks and a white slippery coating. Pulse: deep, slow, and weak.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Yang Deficiency means the body's warming power is low, so cold and dampness easily accumulate. Cold foods and weather further drain Yang, while warmth, rest, and moxibustion gently stoke the internal fire, helping to move fluids and ease the heavy chest pain.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, nourishing foods like ginger, cinnamon, lamb, and chicken soup. Avoid cold drinks and raw salads. Keep the chest and back warm with a scarf or heat pad. Gentle walking helps move fluids, but rest when tired. Moxibustion at home on the abdomen and lower back can be very supportive.

formulas.formula_name: Gua Lou Xie Bai Bai Jiu Tang

formulas.properties: Warm, Unblocks Yang in the Chest, Moves Qi, Expels Phlegm
formulas.description: Warms and unblocks the chest Yang, transforms phlegm and fluids, and relieves distending chest pain.

formulas.translation: Minor Bupleurum Decoction · Eastern Hàn dynasty, circa 200 CE
formulas.properties: Slightly Cool, Harmonizes the Shaoyang, Soothes the Liver and Regulates Qi, Directs Rebellious Qi Downward and Stops Vomiting
formulas.description: A classical formula that harmonises the body when an illness is stuck between the surface and the interior, causing alternating chills and fever, chest and rib-side discomfort, poor appetite, nausea, and irritability. It is one of the most widely used formulas in Chinese medicine, applied to a broad range of conditions involving the Liver, Gallbladder, and digestive system.

formulas.translation: Honeysuckle and Forsythia Powder · Qīng dynasty, 1798 CE
formulas.properties: Cool, Disperses Wind-Heat, Clears Heat, Resolves Toxicity
formulas.description: A classic formula for the early stages of colds and flu caused by Wind-Heat, with symptoms like fever, sore throat, headache, thirst, and cough. It works by gently releasing the exterior to expel the pathogen while clearing heat and resolving toxicity, targeting the upper respiratory system. One of the most widely used formulas in Chinese medicine for acute infections with heat signs.

formulas.translation: Ten-Jujube Decoction · Eastern Hàn dynasty, c. 200 CE
formulas.properties: Cold, Drastically Purges and Expels Water Accumulation, Drains Water and Expels Phlegm-Fluids
formulas.description: A powerful classical formula used to forcefully expel accumulated water and fluid from the chest, flanks, and abdomen. It is designed for severe conditions such as pleural effusion, ascites, or generalized edema in people with a strong constitution. Because its three main herbs are potent and toxic, jujube dates are used to protect the Stomach and moderate the formula's intensity.

formulas.formula_name: Ting Li Da Zao Xie Fei Tang
formulas.translation: Lepidium Seed and Jujube Decoction to Drain the Lungs · Hàn dynasty, ~200 CE
formulas.properties: Cold, Clears Lung Heat, Promotes Bowel and Urinary Movement, Descends Qi and calms wheezing
formulas.description: A small but powerful classical formula with just two ingredients, used to drain accumulated phlegm and fluids from the lungs. It is designed for acute situations where thick phlegm and water congestion cause severe wheezing, chest tightness, difficulty breathing when lying down, and facial swelling. The jujube dates in the formula protect the digestive system from the potent draining action of the Descurainia seeds.

formulas.translation: Drain the White Powder · Northern Sòng dynasty, 1119 CE
formulas.properties: Cool, Clears Lung Heat, Stops Cough, Calms Wheezing
formulas.description: A gentle classical formula originally designed for children to clear hidden heat from the Lungs. It treats coughing, wheezing, and a sensation of warmth in the skin that worsens in the late afternoon, caused by smouldering heat lodged in the Lungs. Its mild, sweet-natured herbs clear Lung heat without harming the body's reserves.

formulas.translation: Minor Trichosanthes Decoction · Eastern Hàn dynasty, ~200 CE
formulas.properties: Cold, Clears Heat and Transforms Phlegm, Broadens the Chest and Dissipates Nodules, Descends Qi and Resolves Binding
formulas.description: A classical three-herb formula used to clear heat and dissolve phlegm that has become stuck in the chest and upper abdomen. It addresses a feeling of tightness, fullness, or pain in the chest or pit of the stomach that worsens with pressure, often accompanied by thick yellow phlegm, a bitter taste, and a greasy yellow tongue coating.

formulas.translation: Drive Out Stasis in the Mansion of Blood Decoction · Qīng dynasty, 1830 CE
formulas.properties: Slightly Warm, Invigorates Blood and Dispels Stasis, Moves Qi and Alleviates Pain, Opens the Chest and Disperses Stagnation
formulas.description: A classical formula designed to improve blood circulation in the chest, relieve pain, and ease emotional tension. It is widely used for chronic chest pain, stubborn headaches, insomnia, and irritability caused by poor blood flow and stagnation in the upper body.

formulas.formula_name: Sha Shen Mai Men Dong Tang
formulas.translation: Glehnia and Ophiopogon Decoction · Qīng dynasty, 1798 CE
formulas.properties: Slightly Cool, Nourishes Lung and Stomach Yin, Generates Fluids, Moistens Dryness
formulas.description: A gentle, cooling formula used to restore moisture and fluids to the Lungs and Stomach when they have become dried out. It is commonly used for persistent dry cough, dry throat, thirst, and other symptoms of dryness, particularly during autumn or following a feverish illness. The formula nourishes without being heavy, making it well-suited for conditions where the body's natural moistening fluids have been depleted.

formulas.translation: Artemisia and Turtle Shell Decoction · Qīng dynasty, 1798 CE
formulas.properties: Cool, Nourishes Yin, Clears Deficiency Heat, Vents Pathogenic Heat Outward
formulas.description: A classical formula for lingering low-grade fevers that come on at night and ease by morning, especially after a prolonged illness. It works by nourishing the body's depleted fluids (Yin) while gently venting trapped heat outward, addressing the root cause of the fever rather than just suppressing symptoms.

formulas.formula_name: Gua Lou Xie Bai Bai Jiu Tang
formulas.translation: Trichosanthes Fruit, Chinese Chive and Wine Decoction · Eastern Hàn dynasty, ~200 CE
formulas.properties: Warm, Unblocks Yang in the Chest, Moves Qi, Expels Phlegm
formulas.description: A classical three-ingredient formula for chest tightness, oppressive chest pain (sometimes radiating to the back), shortness of breath, and wheezing caused by weakened warmth in the chest area combined with phlegm accumulation. It is the foundational prescription in the Gua Lou Xie Bai family of formulas, widely used in modern practice as a base for treating angina and other chest-related conditions.

faqs.question: Can acupuncture really help with pleurisy pain?
faqs.answer: Yes, acupuncture can relieve pleuritic chest pain by reducing inflammation, relaxing the muscles between the ribs, and moving stagnant Qi and Blood in the chest channels. Many patients feel some pain relief after the first few sessions, especially when combined with herbal medicine. The points used-like Shanzhong (REN-17) and Neiguan (PC-6)-directly open the chest and calm the breath. However, if you have a large pleural effusion or severe infection, acupuncture alone is not enough; it works best alongside conventional medical care.

faqs.question: How long do Chinese herbs take to work for pleurisy?
faqs.answer: It depends on the pattern. For an acute infection with fever and sharp pain, herbal formulas can start reducing symptoms within a few days. If there's fluid in the chest, it may take 4-8 weeks to see a noticeable decrease on imaging, though breathing often improves much sooner. Chronic patterns with long-standing stagnation or deficiency need more time-typically 1-3 months for lasting change. Consistency is key: take your herbs daily as prescribed, and don't stop early even if you feel better.

faqs.question: Is it safe to combine TCM with antibiotics or other medications?
faqs.answer: In most cases, yes. TCM can be used alongside antibiotics, anti-inflammatories, or other conventional treatments for pleurisy. The herbal formulas are chosen to complement your medical care, not interfere with it. Always inform both your TCM practitioner and your doctor about all medications and supplements you're taking. If you are on blood thinners or have a history of liver issues, your herbal formula may need adjustments, as some herbs can affect clotting or liver enzymes.

faqs.question: What foods should I avoid when I have pleurisy?
faqs.answer: Generally, you'll want to avoid foods that create dampness and phlegm-cold and raw foods, dairy products, greasy or fried foods, and excessive sweets. These can worsen fluid accumulation and inflammation. Instead, eat warm, cooked, easily digestible meals like soups, congee, and steamed vegetables. If you have a lot of heat (burning pain, yellow phlegm), also avoid spicy foods and alcohol. If you feel cold and weak, warming foods like ginger and cinnamon can help. Your practitioner will give you specific guidance based on your pattern.

faqs.question: Can TCM cure pleurisy permanently?
faqs.answer: TCM aims to not only resolve the current episode but also correct the underlying imbalance that made you susceptible. For many people, especially those with recurrent pleurisy or lingering fluid, this means a lower chance of future episodes. However, 'cure' depends on the root cause-if you have an autoimmune condition or a structural lung problem, TCM can help manage symptoms and reduce flare-ups but may not eliminate the underlying disease. A thorough TCM consultation can give you a realistic picture based on your individual pattern.

faqs.question: What does the tongue and pulse tell a TCM practitioner about pleurisy?
faqs.answer: The tongue and pulse are like a live dashboard of what's happening inside your body. In pleurisy, a red tongue with a yellow coating suggests heat and phlegm, while a pale, swollen tongue with a white slippery coating points to cold fluid accumulation. A wiry pulse often indicates pain and Qi stagnation; a rapid pulse signals heat. By reading these signs, the practitioner confirms the pattern and chooses the most precise acupuncture points and herbal formula for you-it's not guesswork.

research.title: Clinical observation of modified Xiao Chai Hu Tang combined with conventional treatment for tuberculous pleurisy
research.description: This randomized controlled trial included patients with tuberculous pleurisy. The group receiving modified Xiao Chai Hu Tang plus anti-tuberculosis drugs showed faster resolution of pleural effusion and less pleural thickening compared to the control group. The formula was well tolerated with no serious adverse events.
research.periodical: Chinese Journal of Integrated Traditional and Western Medicine, 2015.

research.title: Acupuncture for pleuritic pain: a randomized sham-controlled trial
research.description: This study randomized patients with pleuritic pain to receive either true acupuncture (points: Feishu BL-13, Neiguan PC-6, Shanzhong REN-17) or sham acupuncture. Pain scores decreased significantly more in the true acupuncture group after 5 sessions. The effect persisted at 2-week follow-up.
research.periodical: Journal of Acupuncture and Tuina Science, 2018.

research.title: Ting Li Da Zao Xie Fei Tang for exudative pleurisy: a systematic review of randomized trials
research.description: A meta-analysis of multiple RCTs found that adding Ting Li Da Zao Xie Fei Tang to standard care significantly increased the rate of pleural effusion absorption and shortened the duration of chest pain compared to standard care alone. The quality of the included trials was moderate.
